Wikipedia, Dendritic spike (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dendritic_spike): dendritic nonlinearities and local computations documented in many cell types; a general theory of single-neuron computation stays open

Wikipedia, Convolutional neural network (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network): Yamins and DiCarlo showed in 2014 that deep networks trained for object recognition predict inferior temporal cortex responses; the cortical mechanism stays partly explained
Wikipedia, Mirror neuron (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_neuron): mirror neuron systems documented in monkeys and inferred in humans; their role in perception and understanding stays contested

Wikipedia, Neuroplasticity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroplasticity): Reynolds and Chelazzi reviewed attentional gain changes in V4 in 2004 and Maya Vetencourt restored adult ocular dominance plasticity in rats in 2008; the limits of fast reconfiguration stay open

Wikipedia, Neural correlates of consciousness (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_correlates_of_consciousness): an adversarial collaboration reported in 2023 and 2025 left integrated information and global workspace theories both partly unsupported

Wikipedia, Genome-wide association study (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome-wide_association_study): thousands of trait associations mapped since 2007; common variants explain a minority of heritability for most diseases
no accepted resolution found by 2026; Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in biology (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_biology)

Wikipedia, Induced pluripotent stem cell (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_pluripotent_stem_cell): Yamanaka reprogrammed fibroblasts to pluripotency in 2006; Vierbuchen and Wernig converted fibroblasts directly to neurons in 2010
Wikipedia, Plant tissue culture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_tissue_culture): auxin and cytokinin ratios and WUSCHEL-family regulators identified; the full program stays incomplete

no accepted resolution found by 2026; Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in astronomy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_astronomy)

Wikipedia, Engram (neuropsychology) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engram_(neuropsychology)): optogenetic tagging of engram cells in mice from 2012 shows memory traces can be labelled and reactivated; the general code stays open

Wikipedia, Evolution of cooperation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution_of_cooperation): kin selection, reciprocity and multilevel selection models tested in many systems; the weight of each mechanism stays debated

Wikipedia, AlphaFold (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaFold): machine learning models trained on biological data now predict protein structures and some interactions; whole-cell prediction stays open
no accepted resolution found by 2026; Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in computer_science (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_computer_science)
Wikipedia, Immune tolerance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immune_tolerance): antigen-specific tolerance achieved in animal models and some transplant trials; no routine clinical method
Wikipedia, HIV vaccine development (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV_vaccine_development): no licensed vaccine; RV144 showed partial efficacy in 2009 and later efficacy trials failed
Wikipedia, Climate sensitivity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_sensitivity): Sherwood and colleagues narrowed the likely range to 2.6 to 3.9 K in 2020, adopted by IPCC AR6 in 2021

Wikipedia, Renewable energy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewable_energy): solar and wind became the cheapest new generation in most markets by the early 2020s; liquid fuel replacement for aviation and shipping stays open
no accepted resolution found by 2026; Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in economics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_economics)

Wikipedia, James Webb Space Telescope (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope): JWST from 2022 has confirmed galaxies at redshift above 13, within 300 million years of the big bang; Population III stars remain unobserved

Wikipedia, Ultra-high-energy cosmic ray (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra-high-energy_cosmic_ray): Pierre Auger Observatory found an extragalactic dipole anisotropy in 2017; individual sources are not identified
Wikipedia, Quasar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasar): accretion onto supermassive black holes is the accepted power source; jet launching and accretion physics stay active questions

Wikipedia, Event Horizon Telescope (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_Horizon_Telescope): gravitational waves from merging black holes detected in 2015 and the M87 shadow imaged in 2019 confirm the objects; the information paradox stays open

Wikipedia, Superlens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superlens): near-field superlensing demonstrated at ultraviolet and visible wavelengths from 2005 onward; a far-field perfect lens for visible light has not been built

Wikipedia, Magnetic semiconductor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_semiconductor): room-temperature claims in doped oxides and nitrides stay disputed; no accepted room-temperature dilute magnetic semiconductor

Wikipedia, Island of stability (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_of_stability): elements up to 118 synthesised and flerovium confirmed in 2011; the predicted long-lived isotopes near neutron number 184 have not been reached
Wikipedia, Supersolid (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersolid): the 2004 solid helium claim was withdrawn in 2012; supersolid states were created in dipolar quantum gases in 2019

Wikipedia, Solar-cell efficiency (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar-cell_efficiency): multijunction cells exceed 47 percent under concentration and perovskite-silicon tandems pass 34 percent; cost-effective cells above the single-junction limit stay in development

Wikipedia, National Ignition Facility (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Ignition_Facility): NIF reached fusion ignition with target gain above one in December 2022; no plant produces net electricity

Wikipedia, Nebular hypothesis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebular_hypothesis): ALMA images of protoplanetary disks from 2014 and streaming instability models filled in the growth stages; the metre-size barrier and giant planet timing stay debated

Wikipedia, Milankovitch cycles (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milankovitch_cycles): orbital pacing is accepted and carbon dioxide feedback fills part of the gap; the 100,000-year problem is not fully resolved
Wikipedia, AlphaFold (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaFold): AlphaFold 2 reached experimental accuracy on most CASP14 targets in November 2020

Wikipedia, Human proteome project (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_proteome_project): drafts of the human proteome in 2014 and a 90 percent complete map in 2020 cover protein-coding genes; proteoform counts stay open

Wikipedia, Protein-protein interaction (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein-protein_interaction): structural and kinetic models of encounter complexes and interaction maps have grown; AlphaFold-Multimer predicts many complexes from 2021

Wikipedia, Programmed cell death (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programmed_cell_death): necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis in 2012 and others were defined by the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death; the list continues to grow

Wikipedia, Vesicular transport protein (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesicular_transport_protein): SNARE, Rab and tether machinery mapped, recognised by the 2013 Nobel Prize in medicine; global coordination stays open
Wikipedia, Centrosome cycle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrosome_cycle): PLK4 licensing of centriole duplication identified in 2005 to 2007; the full count control is not settled
Wikipedia, Non-coding RNA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-coding_RNA): microRNA biology recognised by the 2024 Nobel Prize in medicine; functions of most long noncoding RNAs stay uncharacterised

Wikipedia, Telomere-to-telomere consortium (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telomere-to-telomere_consortium): the complete human genome including centromeres was published in 2022; functional roles are still being worked out
Wikipedia, ENCODE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENCODE): ENCODE assigned biochemical activity to most of the genome in 2012; how much of that is functional stays disputed
NHGRI DNA Sequencing Costs data (https://www.genome.gov/about-genomics/fact-sheets/Sequencing-Human-Genome-cost): the cost of a genome fell below 1,500 dollars in 2015 and below 1,000 dollars by 2019

Wikipedia, Hippo signaling pathway (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippo_signaling_pathway): the Hippo pathway identified in the 2000s as a conserved organ size control; systemic size sensing stays incomplete

Wikipedia, Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgenerational_epigenetic_inheritance): mechanisms shown in plants, worms and mice; the extent in humans stays contested

Wikipedia, Left-right asymmetry (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-right_asymmetry): cilia-driven nodal flow and Nodal signalling establish left-right asymmetry in vertebrates; the earliest cue in mammals stays debated

Wikipedia, Evolutionary developmental biology (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_developmental_biology): Hox and Shh enhancer changes link fin to limb and shape beaks and faces; a predictive map is not complete

Wikipedia, Kisspeptin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisspeptin): kisspeptin and KISS1R were shown in 2003 to gate puberty, and MKRN3 mutations in 2013 cause early puberty; the upstream clock stays open
Wikipedia, Cancer stem cell (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer_stem_cell): stem-like cells demonstrated in leukaemia and several solid tumours; the model does not hold for every cancer

Wikipedia, Cancer immunotherapy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer_immunotherapy): the checkpoint inhibitor ipilimumab was approved in 2011 and durable remissions followed, recognised by the 2018 Nobel Prize in medicine
Wikipedia, Targeted therapy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targeted_therapy): imatinib and later targeted drugs keep some cancers controlled for decades; resistance limits most

Wikipedia, Inflammation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflammation): the CANTOS trial in 2017 showed that lowering interleukin-1 beta reduced cardiovascular events; causal roles in other diseases vary
Wikipedia, Prion (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prion): the protein-only hypothesis is accepted and cryo-EM structures of infectious fibrils appeared in 2021; the toxic mechanism stays open

Wikipedia, Innate immune system (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innate_immune_system): Toll-like receptor and inflammasome biology recognised by the 2011 Nobel Prize in medicine; the relative contribution varies by pathogen

Wikipedia, Memory B cell (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_B_cell): long-lived plasma cells and memory cells persist for years in antigen-free mice; the human case is inferred from vaccine studies

Wikipedia, Immune tolerance in pregnancy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immune_tolerance_in_pregnancy): regulatory T cells, HLA-G and decidual natural killer cells identified as mechanisms; no single explanation
Wikipedia, Circadian clock (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circadian_clock): molecular clock mechanisms recognised by the 2017 Nobel Prize in medicine; peripheral clock coordination stays under study
Wikipedia, Magnetoreception (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception): cryptochrome-based magnetic sensing in birds supported by 2021 experiments; the full navigation system is not mapped
Wikipedia, Pheromone (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheromone): no human pheromone has been identified with reproducible behavioural effects

Wikipedia, Causes of schizophrenia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causes_of_schizophrenia): 108 genetic loci mapped in 2014 and complement C4 implicated in 2016; no causal mechanism explains the disorder
Wikipedia, Causes of autism (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causes_of_autism): over 100 risk genes identified and heritability estimated near 80 percent; no single cause or biomarker
Wikipedia, Lecanemab (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecanemab): anti-amyloid antibodies lecanemab and donanemab approved in 2023 and 2024 slow decline by about a quarter over 18 months
Wikipedia, Addiction (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addiction): dopamine reward circuit changes and genetic risk factors characterised; the transition to compulsive use is not fully explained

Wikipedia, Neuroscience of morality (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroscience_of_morality): imaging links moral judgement to prefrontal and limbic networks; whether these are dedicated circuits stays contested

Wikipedia, Heritability of personality (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritability_of_personality): twin studies give heritabilities near 40 to 50 percent; genome-wide studies explain a small fraction

Wikipedia, Biology and sexual orientation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology_and_sexual_orientation): a 2019 study of nearly 500,000 genomes found several loci with small effects; prenatal factors remain under study

Wikipedia, Phylogenetic tree (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogenetic_tree): genome-scale phylogenies settled many branches, with a 2016 tree of life proposed; deep relationships such as eukaryote origins stay debated

Wikipedia, Horizontal gene transfer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizontal_gene_transfer): transfer mechanisms such as conjugation, transduction and transformation are well described; its evolutionary weight in eukaryotes stays debated

Wikipedia, Last universal common ancestor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_universal_common_ancestor): comparative genomics in 2016 and 2024 placed LUCA about 4.2 billion years ago as an anaerobic thermophile-like cell; details stay inferred

Wikipedia, Flowering plant (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_plant): the Amborella genome in 2013 and fossil finds narrowed the origin to the Early Cretaceous or before; the ancestral flower stays reconstructed
Wikipedia, Cell wall (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_wall): cellulose synthase complexes imaged and lignin pathways mapped; wall assembly is not fully understood
Wikipedia, Plant hormone (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_hormone): gibberellin and brassinosteroid signalling explain Green Revolution dwarfing; size regulation across species stays open

Wikipedia, Plant disease resistance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_disease_resistance): the zigzag model of pattern-triggered and effector-triggered immunity set in 2006; resistance gene networks stay under study
Wikipedia, Abiotic stress (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abiotic_stress): many stress tolerance genes and DREB regulators mapped; polygenic tolerance has resisted simple transfer

Wikipedia, Extinction event (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinction_event): volcanism and climate change implicated in the end-Permian and end-Triassic events; the Ordovician and Devonian causes stay debated
Wikipedia, Sauropoda (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropoda): air sacs, long necks and egg laying proposed in 2011 as the combination enabling gigantism; the model is not complete

Wikipedia, Effects of climate change on biomes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_climate_change_on_biomes): range shifts and phenology changes documented across thousands of species; ecosystem-level prediction stays uncertain

Wikipedia, Denisovan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan): Denisovans identified from DNA in 2010 and Homo naledi and Homo luzonensis described later; interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans is established

Wikipedia, Human genetic variation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_genetic_variation): genome studies show continuous variation structured by geography; the biological meaning of race is rejected while ancestry structure is mapped

Wikipedia, Economy of Africa (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Africa): life expectancy rose and extreme poverty rates fell after 2005 as antiretroviral coverage and growth spread; causes stay debated

Wikipedia, YInMn Blue (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YInMn_Blue): YInMn blue discovered in 2009 and approved for commercial use in 2020; a stable inorganic red remains sought

Wikipedia, Retrosynthetic analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrosynthetic_analysis): machine learning retrosynthesis tools and self-driving labs in use from the late 2010s; autonomous discovery remains limited
Wikipedia, Common cold (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_cold): no vaccine or cure; antiviral candidates have not reached approval

Wikipedia, Personalized medicine (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personalized_medicine): an antisense drug was made for one child in 2018 and personalised CRISPR therapy treated an infant in 2025; routine individual manufacture is not established
Wikipedia, Meridian (Chinese medicine) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_(Chinese_medicine)): no anatomical structure corresponding to meridians has been identified

Wikipedia, MRNA vaccine (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRNA_vaccine): mRNA vaccines were authorised in December 2020 within a year of the SARS-CoV-2 sequence; universal and mucosal vaccines stay in development

Wikipedia, Causes of autism (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causes_of_autism): Satterstrom and colleagues mapped 102 risk genes from 35,584 exomes in 2020 and Bai estimated heritability near 80 percent in 2019; no single cause or biomarker

Wikipedia, Cellular differentiation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellular_differentiation): chromatin and transcription factor barriers to reprogramming described; the full logic of fate restriction stays open

Wikipedia, Human-canine bond (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human-canine_bond): mutual oxytocin release in gazing between dogs and owners reported in 2015; a general account stays open
Wikipedia, De-extinction (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De-extinction): a Pyrenean ibex clone lived minutes in 2003; gene-edited wolves marketed as dire wolves in 2025 are disputed as de-extinction

Wikipedia, Projections of population growth (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projections_of_population_growth): UN 2024 projections peak near 10.3 billion in the 2080s; the timing depends on fertility trends
Wikipedia, Epiphyseal plate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphyseal_plate): oestrogen-driven growth plate fusion and senescence of the plate are established; the systemic size set point stays open
Wikipedia, Hibernation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibernation): torpor induced in mice by neuronal stimulation in 2020; no human hibernation demonstrated

Wikipedia, Exagamglogene autotemcel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exagamglogene_autotemcel): the first CRISPR therapy was approved for sickle cell disease in 2023; in vivo editing for many diseases stays in trials

Wikipedia, Synthetic biology (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_biology): a synthetic genome booted a cell in 2010 and a minimal cell JCVI-syn3.0 followed in 2016, both using an existing cell body; a fully synthetic cell has not been made

Wikipedia, Biomolecular condensate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomolecular_condensate): phase-separated condensates recognised since 2009 as an organising principle; a general theory of intracellular organisation stays open
Wikipedia, Shape of the universe (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape_of_the_universe): Planck data constrain curvature to near zero; topology and finiteness are not determined
Wikipedia, Colonization of Mars (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization_of_Mars): no crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit since 1972; settlement proposals remain plans

Wikipedia, Supermassive black hole (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermassive_black_hole): stellar collapse and mergers are established; the rapid growth of early supermassive black holes seen by JWST stays unexplained

Wikipedia, Stability of the Solar System (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_of_the_Solar_System): numerical integrations show chaos with a one percent chance of Mercury-Venus collision over five billion years; long-term stability is probabilistic
Wikipedia, Cosmic ray (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray): supernova remnants confirmed as sources of galactic cosmic rays in 2013; the highest-energy sources are not identified
Wikipedia, Higgs boson (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson): the Higgs boson discovered in 2012 explains how particles acquire mass; the values of the masses are not explained

Wikipedia, Tests of general relativity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity): gravitational waves and black hole shadows match predictions; quantum gravity and cosmological tensions stay open
Wikipedia, Pulsar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulsar): formation in core-collapse supernovae and spin-up by accretion are established; the emission mechanism stays open

Wikipedia, Deep biosphere (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_biosphere): the Deep Carbon Observatory estimated 15 to 23 billion tonnes of carbon in deep life in 2018; composition and function stay partly known
Wikipedia, Neutron star (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_star): gravitational wave event GW170817 in 2017 and NICER measurements constrain the equation of state; the core composition stays open

Wikipedia, IceCube Neutrino Observatory (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IceCube_Neutrino_Observatory): the blazar TXS 0506+056 in 2018 and the galaxy NGC 1068 in 2022 identified as sources; most of the flux is unattributed
Wikipedia, R-process (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R-process): the neutron star merger GW170817 in 2017 produced r-process elements; the share from mergers versus rare supernovae stays debated

Wikipedia, Super-resolution microscopy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super-resolution_microscopy): fluorescence methods beat the limit, recognised by the 2014 Nobel Prize in chemistry; the limit holds for conventional far-field imaging
Wikipedia, Bose-Einstein condensate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bose-Einstein_condensate): condensates run in orbit since 2018 and in atom interferometers; everyday devices do not use them

Wikipedia, Metamaterial cloaking (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamaterial_cloaking): microwave and small-scale optical cloaks demonstrated since 2006; broadband visible cloaking of large objects stays undemonstrated
Wikipedia, Self-driving car (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-driving_car): driverless robotaxis operate commercially in several cities since 2020; full autonomy in all conditions is not achieved

Wikipedia, DNA digital data storage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_digital_data_storage): megabytes stored and recovered since 2012 and random access shown in 2018; cost keeps it from production use

Wikipedia, Artificial intelligence in healthcare (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_in_healthcare): AI matches specialists on narrow imaging tasks and some approved tools exist; general clinical replacement is not demonstrated

Wikipedia, Topological quantum computer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_quantum_computer): Majorana zero mode claims in 2018 were retracted and 2025 claims stay disputed; no topological qubit demonstrated beyond dispute
Wikipedia, Origin of speech (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_speech): Broca's and Wernicke's areas and FOXP2 are established; the evolutionary timeline stays contested

Wikipedia, Dynamo theory (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamo_theory): convective dynamo simulations reproduce a dipole field and reversals since 1995; the energy budget and inner core age stay debated

Wikipedia, Weather forecasting (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_forecasting): hurricane track forecasts improved and machine learning models matched physical models in 2023; earthquake prediction stays out of reach

Wikipedia, Sea level rise (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level_rise): total melt would raise sea level about 70 metres; the timescale under current warming spans millennia with ice sheet dynamics uncertain
Wikipedia, Cold fusion (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_fusion): no reproducible evidence since the 1989 claims; a 2019 Google-funded search found none

Wikipedia, Brain-computer interface (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain-computer_interface): implanted interfaces restore cursor control and speech in paralysed patients since the 2000s; cognitive enhancement is not demonstrated

Wikipedia, Computational creativity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_creativity): generative models produce text, images and music judged novel since 2022; whether this matches human creativity stays debated

rows.t: Energy source behind the age of the Earth
rows.st: What unknown energy source lets the Earth and Sun last far longer than the tens of millions of years that Kelvin calculated from cooling and contraction?
Is there a mechanical procedure that takes any statement of first-order logic and decides in finitely many steps whether it is universally valid, as Hilbert and Ackermann asked in 1928?
Since graph isomorphism is neither known to be NP-complete nor known to be solvable in polynomial time, can it be decided in quasi-polynomial time, faster than any previously known algorithm?

rows.t: Maximum moves to solve a Rubik's Cube
rows.st: Is the number of moves needed to solve the worst Rubik's Cube position, given an ideal algorithm, in the low twenties as Singmaster and Frey hypothesised in 1982, and what is its exact value?
Does there exist an encryption scheme that allows arbitrary computation on ciphertexts without decrypting them, a problem raised in 1978 shortly after the RSA scheme was published?
Can a program be obfuscated so that equivalent programs become indistinguishable, using only well-founded assumptions such as learning with errors, as the 2001 definition of indistinguishability…
Can it be decided in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime or composite, without relying on unproved hypotheses such as the generalized Riemann hypothesis?
Is the traditional schoolbook method of multiplying two n-digit numbers in about n squared steps asymptotically optimal, as Kolmogorov conjectured, or can fewer digit operations suffice?
Can the linear programming problem be solved in time polynomial in the size of its input, a question left open even though the simplex method worked well in practice?

rows.t: Machine victory over a top Go professional
rows.st: Can a computer program defeat a top professional human player at the full-size game of Go, long considered a far harder challenge than chess for artificial intelligence?

rows.t: Maxwell's demon and the cost of information
rows.st: Can a small being that sorts fast and slow molecules without doing work defeat the second law of thermodynamics, as Maxwell imagined in 1867, and what prevents it?
Can the 129-digit number in the 1977 RSA factoring challenge be factored, so that its encrypted message is read, despite the belief that factoring such numbers is infeasible?
Does the nerve impulse cross the synapse as an electrical current or by the release of a chemical messenger, a question that divided physiologists before the early 1920s?
Does the hippocampus hold a spatial representation of the environment, and do individual neurons there fire at particular locations as an animal moves through space?
Can memories be stored by strengthening existing connections between neurons, as Ramon y Cajal proposed in 1894, and is there a lasting increase in synaptic strength after activity?
Can all cells of one type in the brain be controlled while leaving the others unaltered, as Francis Crick asked in 1979, perhaps by using light with millisecond precision?
Could ordinary people who simply followed orders be led to harm others, as Eichmann and his accomplices claimed, and how far will obedience to an authority extend?
Does a heavier isotope of hydrogen exist, with a nucleus carrying the proton charge but about twice its mass, as Rutherford suggested in 1920 and spectroscopists looked for?
Does the nucleus contain an electrically neutral particle of about the proton mass, as Rutherford predicted in 1920, to account for nuclear masses and charges without electrons inside the nucleus?
Does the positive counterpart of the electron that follows from Dirac's relativistic wave equation of 1927 exist as a real particle that can be seen in cosmic rays or laboratory tracks?
Does a meson of intermediate mass exist that carries the nuclear force between protons and neutrons, as Yukawa predicted in 1935, and can it be found among cosmic ray particles?
Can the neutrino that Pauli proposed in 1930 to rescue energy conservation in beta decay be detected, given that it should interact with matter almost never?
Do protons contain point-like internal constituents, as the quark model of Gell-Mann and Zweig predicted in 1964, and can deep inelastic electron scattering reveal them?
Does a fourth quark flavour called charm exist, as Bjorken and Glashow proposed in 1964, and would it appear as a narrow heavy meson in high-energy collisions?
Does a fifth quark flavour called bottom exist, as the Kobayashi and Maskawa scheme of 1973 requires, and would it show up as a heavy bound quark pair?
Do the heavy W and Z bosons that the electroweak theory of Glashow, Salam and Weinberg requires exist, and can a proton-antiproton collider produce them?
How does light eject electrons from a metal surface, an effect reported by Hertz in 1887 whose dependence on frequency rather than intensity classical wave theory could not explain?

rows.t: Possibility of a nuclear chain reaction
rows.st: Is a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction possible, as Szilard suspected in 1934, so that neutrons released by one fission could trigger further fissions in uranium?

rows.t: Bright spot behind a circular shadow
rows.st: If light is a wave, does diffraction put a bright spot at the centre of the shadow of a circular disc, as Poisson argued in 1818 against the wave theory?
Do electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light exist as Maxwell's field theory predicts, and can they be generated and detected with an electric spark apparatus in a laboratory?
Why does classical radiation theory predict infinite energy from a heated black body at short wavelengths, and what modification of the theory gives the finite spectrum that is measured?

rows.t: Earth motion through the luminiferous aether
rows.st: Does the Earth move through a stationary luminiferous aether, so that the speed of light measured on Earth varies with the direction of the Earth's motion through that medium?

rows.t: DARPA Grand Challenge, autonomous desert driving
rows.st: Can a fully autonomous ground vehicle complete a 200 kilometre off-road desert course within ten hours with no human intervention?
Can an autonomous vehicle drive 96 kilometres through urban traffic obeying traffic law, merging, parking and negotiating intersections with other vehicles?
Can a team locate ten red weather balloons moored at undisclosed sites across the continental United States within a day using the internet and social networks?
Can shredded documents cut into more than 10,000 pieces be reconstructed from images well enough to solve the puzzles written on them?
Can a backpack-portable unmanned aircraft fly quietly into a site, perch and conduct three hours of surveillance, then return, built by a crowd-sourced team?
Can a distributed team design the drivetrain and mobility system of an infantry fighting vehicle using collaborative model-based tools within months?
Can a software-defined radio deliver data over a shared channel in the presence of other users and interfering signals better than competing radios?
Can modellers accurately forecast the number of chikungunya cases in every Western Hemisphere country between September 2014 and March 2015?
Can a semi-autonomous ground robot drive a vehicle, open doors, climb stairs, turn valves and complete other disaster-response tasks in a degraded human environment?
Can a fully automatic system find, prove and patch software vulnerabilities in real time in a capture-the-flag contest with no human intervention?
Can radios driven by machine learning share crowded spectrum collaboratively, without preset allocations, and carry more traffic than fixed assignment?
Can a team of robots autonomously map, traverse and search tunnels, urban underground spaces and natural caves without GPS or reliable communications?
Can a small launch provider put satellites into low Earth orbit twice within days from different sites with little advance notice of payload and orbit?

rows.t: DARPA Forecasting Floats in Turbulence Challenge
rows.st: Can the positions of ocean drifters be predicted ten days ahead from their tracks and ocean data?
Can systems built on large language models find and patch vulnerabilities across millions of lines of open-source code without human help?
Can autonomous sensors and algorithms identify which casualties at a mass-casualty scene need care most urgently, as fast and as well as medics?

rows.t: Chemistry enabling an economically viable CO2 capture, utilization, and storage strategy
rows.st: Can chemistry make carbon dioxide capture, use and storage economically viable at the scale of global emissions?

rows.t: Fast electron and cation coupled transport within inorganic ionic matrices
rows.st: Can fast coupled transport of electrons and cations in inorganic solids be understood and designed for better batteries and fuel cells?

rows.t: Catalysts by design: the power of theory
rows.st: Can theory and computation design a new catalyst from first principles that then performs as predicted in the laboratory?

rows.t: Ab initio reactive computer aided molecular design
rows.st: Can molecules with a specified reactivity be designed entirely by first-principles computation before any synthesis is attempted in the laboratory?

rows.t: Ammonia as an ultimate amino source in transition metal-catalyzed C-H amination
rows.st: Can ammonia itself be used as the nitrogen source for direct catalytic amination of carbon-hydrogen bonds?
Can the full set of conformations of every protein in the proteome be measured or predicted to understand function?

rows.t: Site-selective bond activation under catalyst control
rows.st: Can a catalyst select one carbon-hydrogen bond among many similar ones in a complex molecule for functionalisation?

rows.t: Cost-effective and sustainable use of precious metals in heterogeneous catalysts
rows.st: Can heterogeneous catalysts use precious metals at single-atom efficiency or replace them with earth-abundant elements at equal performance?

rows.t: Swallowing a surgeon: toward clinical nanorobots
rows.st: Can nanoscale robots be built that operate inside the body to diagnose and treat disease?

rows.t: Efficient and stable perovskite solar cells
rows.st: Can perovskite solar cells reach commercial efficiency with the operational stability of silicon over decades?

rows.t: Solar fuels and solar chemicals industry
rows.st: Can sunlight drive the production of fuels and chemicals from water and carbon dioxide at industrial scale and cost?
Can alkanes from natural gas and petroleum be functionalised selectively at scale under mild conditions?

rows.t: Holy grails for computational organic chemistry and biochemistry
rows.st: Can computation predict the outcome, rate and selectivity of any organic or enzymatic reaction accurately before it is run?

rows.t: Designing polymer electrolytes for safe and high capacity rechargeable lithium batteries
rows.st: Can a solid polymer electrolyte give lithium batteries high conductivity, safety and capacity at room temperature?

rows.t: Computational catalyst design: feasible or fiction?
rows.st: Is purely computational design of a working catalyst feasible, and under what conditions does it succeed?

rows.t: Semiconductor surface chemistry in photocatalysis and photovoltaics
rows.st: Can the surface chemistry of semiconductors be controlled well enough to make efficient and durable photocatalysts and photovoltaics?

rows.t: Controlling silica in its crystalline and amorphous states
rows.st: Can the structure of silica be controlled at the atomic level in both crystalline and amorphous forms for designed materials?

rows.t: Transition from prebiotic chemistry to protobiology
rows.st: Which chemical pathway carried the early Earth from prebiotic molecules to the first self-sustaining protocells?
Can materials be made that incorporate living cells and keep the ability to grow, sense and repair themselves?
Can porous materials such as metal-organic frameworks be designed for industrial gas separation, storage and catalysis at scale?

rows.t: Two-dimensional conjugated polymers based on C-C coupling
rows.st: Can large, defect-free two-dimensional conjugated polymers be synthesised through carbon-carbon coupling reactions in solution or on surfaces?
Can energy materials such as battery electrodes and solar absorbers be made to repair their own damage during operation?
Can nanoparticle medicines deliver drugs to targeted tissues in patients with the precision shown in animal models?

rows.t: Sea spray aerosol as the chemical link between oceans, atmosphere, and climate
rows.st: Can the chemistry of sea spray aerosol be understood well enough to predict its effect on clouds and climate?
Can the inorganic chemistry of metals in neurons explain neural activity and, in the end, consciousness?

rows.t: Ultrasensitive molecular and cellular analysis to speed diagnosis of disease
rows.st: Can single-molecule and single-cell analysis methods make disease diagnosis faster and simpler at the point of care?

rows.t: Shall we even understand the fly's brain?
rows.st: Can the roughly 100,000 neurons of the fly brain be understood as a complete circuit that explains the animal's behaviour?

rows.t: Can we understand the action of brain in natural environments?
rows.st: Can neural processing be understood under natural stimuli and free behaviour rather than simplified laboratory conditions?

rows.t: Which brain functions are lateralized and why?
rows.st: Which functions are assigned to one cerebral hemisphere, and what evolutionary or developmental reason produces that asymmetry?

rows.t: What is the function of the thalamus?
rows.st: What does the thalamus do beyond relaying sensory input to cortex, and how do its first-order and higher-order nuclei shape cortical processing?

rows.t: What is a neuronal map, how does it arise, and what is it good for?
rows.st: How do topographic neuronal maps form during development, and what computational advantage do they give the brain?

rows.t: What is the role of top-down connections?
rows.st: What do the feedback connections from higher to lower cortical areas compute, given that they outnumber the feedforward ones?

rows.t: How fast is neuronal signal transmission?
rows.st: How fast can a population of neurons transmit a signal change, and what limits that speed in cortical circuits?

rows.t: What is the origin and function of irregular neural activity?
rows.st: Why is cortical spiking so irregular, and does that variability serve a computational function or reflect noise?

rows.t: Are single cortical neurons independent or members of a huge orchestra?
rows.st: Is the response of a single cortical neuron set by its own input, or dominated by the ongoing coordinated activity of the population it belongs to?

rows.t: What is the other 85 percent of V1 doing?
rows.st: What computation do the many primary visual cortex neurons that classical receptive field models fail to explain carry out?

rows.t: What is the formal computation in early vision?
rows.st: What formal computation does early vision perform on retinal input, and can it be stated as a mathematical problem?
How do dendrites, synapses and ion channels combine to perform computations within a single neuron?

rows.t: How can neural systems compute in the time domain?
rows.st: How do neural circuits measure and compute with time intervals that range from microseconds in sound localisation to seconds in behaviour?
Are the same coding strategies used across sensory systems and species, or does each system use its own code?

rows.t: How does the hearing system perform auditory scene analysis?
rows.st: How does the auditory system separate overlapping sounds from different sources into distinct perceived streams?

rows.t: How does our visual system achieve shift and size invariance?
rows.st: How does the visual system recognise objects regardless of their position and size on the retina?

rows.t: What is reflected in sensory neocortical activity?
rows.st: Does activity in sensory cortex represent the external stimulus or what the cortex is doing with it for the animal's task?

rows.t: To what extent does perception depend upon action?
rows.st: How far does perception depend on the motor system, as mirror neurons and action-based accounts of understanding suggest?

rows.t: What are the projective fields of cortical neurons?
rows.st: What effect does a single cortical neuron's output have on its downstream targets, the projective field complementing its receptive field?

rows.t: To what extent is the brain reconfigurable?
rows.st: How much can attention and context reconfigure cortical circuits on fast timescales, and by what mechanisms?

rows.t: Where are the switches on this thing?
rows.st: What mechanisms switch brain circuits between modes of operation, routing signals to different targets and gating when plasticity can occur?

rows.t: Do qualia, metaphor, language, and abstract thought emerge from synesthesia?
rows.st: Does cross-wiring between brain maps, as in synaesthesia, explain the origin of metaphor, language and abstract thought?

rows.t: What are the neural correlates of consciousness?
rows.st: Which minimal neural mechanisms are jointly sufficient for a conscious percept, and how can they be identified experimentally?

rows.t: What Is the Universe Made Of?
rows.st: What are the dark matter and dark energy that together make up about 95 percent of the mass and energy of the universe?

rows.t: What is the Biological Basis of Consciousness?
rows.st: Which physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective conscious experience, and how could that correspondence be measured and explained?

rows.t: Why Do Humans Have So Few Genes?
rows.st: How can about 20,000 protein-coding genes build a human when simpler organisms carry a similar number, and where does the extra complexity come from?

rows.t: To What Extent Are Genetic Variation and Personal Health Linked?
rows.st: How much of the variation in disease risk and drug response between people can be traced to inherited genetic differences, and which variants matter?

rows.t: Can the Laws of Physics Be Unified?
rows.st: Can gravity and the three quantum forces of the Standard Model be described by one consistent theory, and can such a theory be tested?

rows.t: How Much Can Human Life Span Be Extended?
rows.st: Is there a fixed upper limit to human life span, and can interventions that extend life in animals be made to work in people?
Which signals let salamanders and zebrafish regrow limbs and hearts, and why do mammals lack that ability for most organs?

rows.t: How Can a Skin Cell Become a Nerve Cell?
rows.st: Can a differentiated somatic cell such as a skin fibroblast be reprogrammed into a neuron or another cell type without passing through an embryo?

rows.t: How Does a Single Somatic Cell Become a Whole Plant?
rows.st: What lets one differentiated plant cell dedifferentiate and regenerate an entire plant, and which genes and hormones switch that program on?
How do convection in the mantle, the dynamo in the core and plate motion at the surface fit into one account of the planet's interior?

rows.t: Are We Alone in the Universe?
rows.st: Does life, intelligent or otherwise, exist anywhere beyond Earth, and how could its presence be detected from astronomical or planetary data?

rows.t: How and Where Did Life on Earth Arise?
rows.st: By what chemical steps, in which environment and at what time did self-replicating life first arise on the early Earth?
Why do some regions and lineages hold so many more species than others, and which ecological and evolutionary forces set those numbers?

rows.t: What Genetic Changes Made Us Uniquely Human?
rows.st: Which changes in the genome separate humans from chimpanzees and other apes and account for human-specific traits such as language and a large brain?

rows.t: How Are Memories Stored and Retrieved?
rows.st: In what physical form does the brain hold a memory, how is it consolidated, and how is the same trace found and read out again later?
How can natural selection favour individuals that help others at a cost to themselves, from microbes to human societies?

rows.t: How Will Big Pictures Emerge from a Sea of Biological Data?
rows.st: Can the flood of genomic, proteomic and imaging data be turned into predictive models of cells and organisms rather than catalogues?

rows.t: How Far Can We Push Chemical Self-Assembly?
rows.st: Can molecules be designed to assemble themselves into functional structures as complex as those living cells build?

rows.t: What Are the Limits of Conventional Computing?
rows.st: How far can silicon transistor scaling continue, and which problems lie beyond the reach of any classical computer in principle?

rows.t: Can We Selectively Shut Off Immune Responses?
rows.st: Can the immune system be made to tolerate one antigen, such as a transplanted organ or an autoimmune target, while keeping the rest of its defences?

rows.t: Do Deeper Principles Underlie Quantum Uncertainty and Nonlocality?
rows.st: Is there a deeper principle from which the uncertainty and nonlocal correlations of quantum mechanics follow, or are they fundamental?

rows.t: Is an Effective HIV Vaccine Feasible?
rows.st: Can a vaccine be designed that gives durable protection against infection by the fast-mutating human immunodeficiency virus?

rows.t: How Hot Will the Greenhouse World Be?
rows.st: By how much will global mean temperature rise for a doubling of atmospheric carbon dioxide, and can the range of climate sensitivity be narrowed?

rows.t: What Can Replace Cheap Oil, and When?
rows.st: Which energy sources can replace petroleum at comparable cost and scale for transport and industry, and on what timeline?

rows.t: Will Malthus Continue to Be Wrong?
rows.st: Can food, water and energy production keep pace with a population heading toward 9 to 10 billion without collapse of the systems that supply them?
Is the observable universe one region of a larger multiverse, and could any observation ever distinguish that from a single universe?
Which field or mechanism drove the exponential expansion of the early universe, and which observable signatures could identify it?

rows.t: When and how did the first stars and galaxies form?
rows.st: When did the first stars and galaxies form after the big bang, and how did they assemble from primordial gas?

rows.t: Where do ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays come from?
rows.st: Which astrophysical sources accelerate cosmic rays to energies above 10^19 electronvolts, given that such particles cannot travel far before losing energy?
How does matter falling onto a supermassive black hole produce the luminosity and jets of a quasar, and what sets the details of that engine?

rows.t: What is the nature of black holes?
rows.st: What happens to matter and information inside a black hole, and how do general relativity and quantum mechanics combine at its horizon and singularity?

rows.t: Why is there more matter than antimatter?
rows.st: What process in the early universe produced the excess of matter over antimatter that left the matter we observe today?
Does the proton decay as grand unified theories predict, and if so what is its lifetime?

rows.t: What is the nature of gravity?
rows.st: How does gravity fit with quantum theory, and is there a graviton or another structure beneath general relativity?

rows.t: Why is time different from other dimensions?
rows.st: Why does time have a direction and behave differently from the three spatial dimensions in physical law and in experience?

rows.t: Are there smaller building blocks than quarks?
rows.st: Are quarks and leptons composite objects built from smaller constituents, and at what energy would such structure appear?
Is the neutrino a Majorana particle identical to its antiparticle, as a detection of neutrinoless double beta decay would show?

rows.t: Is there a unified theory explaining all correlated electron systems?
rows.st: Can one theory describe the collective behaviour of electrons in high-temperature superconductors, heavy fermion metals and colossal magnetoresistance materials?

rows.t: What is the most powerful laser researchers can build?
rows.st: Is there an upper limit to laser intensity set by vacuum pair production, and how close can petawatt and exawatt facilities get to it?

rows.t: Can researchers make a perfect optical lens?
rows.st: Can a negative-index material focus visible light below the diffraction limit as a perfect lens, as it already does for microwaves?

rows.t: Is it possible to create magnetic semiconductors that work at room temperature?
rows.st: Can a semiconductor be made ferromagnetic at room temperature so that spin and charge can be controlled together in spintronic devices?

rows.t: What is the pairing mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity?
rows.st: What binds electrons into pairs in cuprate and other high-temperature superconductors, where the phonon mechanism of conventional superconductors does not apply?

rows.t: Can we develop a general theory of turbulent flows and granular motion?
rows.st: Is there a general statistical theory for far-from-equilibrium systems such as turbulent fluids and flowing granular materials?
Is there an island of stability of long-lived superheavy nuclei near 114 protons and 184 neutrons, and can such nuclei be made?

rows.t: Is superfluidity possible in a solid?
rows.st: Can a crystalline material flow without friction as a supersolid, combining the order of a solid with the superflow of a superfluid?

rows.t: What is the structure of water?
rows.st: How many hydrogen bonds does each water molecule form with its neighbours in the liquid, and how is that network arranged and rearranged?

rows.t: What is the nature of the glassy state?
rows.st: What distinguishes a glass from a liquid at the molecular level, and is the glass transition a true phase transition?

rows.t: Are there limits to rational chemical synthesis?
rows.st: How large and complex a molecule can chemists make by design with control of shape and in useful quantity, and where does that control fail?

rows.t: What is the ultimate efficiency of photovoltaic cells?
rows.st: Can solar cells convert more than the single-junction limit of about 32 percent of sunlight into electricity at practical cost?

rows.t: Will fusion always be the energy source of the future?
rows.st: Can controlled nuclear fusion produce net energy and become a practical electricity source within decades rather than receding indefinitely?

rows.t: What drives the solar magnetic cycle?
rows.st: Which dynamo process inside the Sun produces the 22-year magnetic cycle, and why do simulations fail to reproduce it in detail?
How do dust and gas in a disk around a young star grow into planets before the material is lost to the star or dispersed?
How do changes in Earth's orbit and tilt trigger the 100,000-year glacial cycles, given that the orbital forcing alone looks too weak?

rows.t: What causes reversals in Earth's magnetic field?
rows.st: Why does the geodynamo reverse polarity at irregular intervals, and can simulations and paleomagnetic data explain the timing?

rows.t: Are there earthquake precursors that can lead to useful predictions?
rows.st: Do measurable signals precede large earthquakes in a way that allows one to predict their time, place and size?

rows.t: Is there, or was there, life elsewhere in the solar system?
rows.st: Did life ever arise on Mars, Europa, Enceladus or another body in the solar system, and does any of it persist today?

rows.t: What is the origin of homochirality in nature?
rows.st: Why do living organisms use only left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars, and what broke the mirror symmetry before life began?

rows.t: Can we predict how proteins will fold?
rows.st: Can the three-dimensional structure a protein adopts be predicted from its amino acid sequence alone with accuracy comparable to experiment?

rows.t: How many proteins are there in humans?
rows.st: How many distinct proteins, counting splice variants and modifications, does the human body make, and can they all be catalogued?

rows.t: How do proteins find their partners?
rows.st: How do two proteins locate each other and bind in the right orientation within seconds inside a crowded cell?

rows.t: How many forms of cell death are there?
rows.st: How many distinct programmed pathways can kill a cell beyond apoptosis and necrosis, and how are they related?

rows.t: What keeps intracellular traffic on course?
rows.st: How do membrane vesicles inside a cell find the right compartment and fuse there without sticking to or losing their way among other membranes?

rows.t: What enables cellular components to copy themselves independent of DNA?
rows.st: How do centrosomes and other organelles duplicate once per cell cycle on their own schedule without a DNA template?

rows.t: What roles do different forms of RNA play in genome function?
rows.st: Which functions do noncoding RNAs such as microRNAs and long noncoding RNAs carry out in regulating the genome?

rows.t: What role do telomeres and centromeres play in genome function?
rows.st: What do the repetitive telomere and centromere regions of chromosomes do, given that they could not be sequenced with earlier technology?

rows.t: Why are some genomes big and others compact?
rows.st: Why does genome size vary by orders of magnitude between organisms of similar complexity, and what is the selective or neutral explanation?

rows.t: What is all that junk doing in our genomes?
rows.st: What function, if any, does the noncoding DNA between genes serve in genome regulation, evolution and species differences?

rows.t: How much will new technologies lower the cost of sequencing?
rows.st: Can the cost of sequencing a human genome fall by orders of magnitude, to around 1,000 dollars, through new sequencing technologies?

rows.t: How do organs and whole organisms know when to stop growing?
rows.st: Which signals tell an organ or body that it has reached the right size and should stop growing?

rows.t: How can genome changes other than mutations be inherited?
rows.st: By what molecular mechanisms are epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation passed between generations, and how stable is that inheritance?

rows.t: How is asymmetry determined in the embryo?
rows.st: What first breaks the symmetry of a uniform ball of embryonic cells to set the body's left-right, head-tail and back-front axes?

rows.t: How do limbs, fins, and faces develop and evolve?
rows.st: How do genetic programs shape limbs, fins and faces during development, and how did changes in those programs drive their evolution?
Which signal starts puberty by reactivating the hypothalamic reproductive axis after childhood, and how do nutrition and genes set its timing?

rows.t: Are stem cells at the heart of all cancers?
rows.st: Are all tumours driven by a small population of cancer stem cells, so that killing those cells would eliminate the cancer?

rows.t: Is cancer susceptible to immune control?
rows.st: Can the immune system be made to recognise and destroy established tumours despite the countermeasures cancer cells use to evade it?

rows.t: Can cancers be controlled rather than cured?
rows.st: Can tumours be held in check for years as a chronic condition by drugs that cut their blood supply or growth signals?

rows.t: Is inflammation a major factor in all chronic diseases?
rows.st: Does chronic inflammation drive heart disease, cancer and other chronic diseases, and if so by which mechanisms?
How does a misfolded prion protein travel from gut to brain, convert normal protein and kill neurons?

rows.t: How much do vertebrates depend on the innate immune system to fight infection?
rows.st: How much of vertebrate defence against infection rests on the older innate immune system rather than on adaptive antibodies and T cells?

rows.t: Does immunologic memory require chronic exposure to antigens?
rows.st: Do memory lymphocytes persist for decades without any re-exposure to their antigen, or does low-level antigen persistence maintain them?

rows.t: Why doesn't a pregnant woman reject her fetus?
rows.st: How does the maternal immune system tolerate a fetus carrying foreign paternal antigens for nine months while still fighting infection?

rows.t: What synchronizes an organism's circadian clocks?
rows.st: How are the circadian clocks found in nearly every cell of the body kept in step with one another and with the day?

rows.t: How do migrating organisms find their way?
rows.st: Which sensory cues and neural mechanisms let birds, butterflies and whales steer journeys of thousands of kilometres?
What function does sleep serve that makes it necessary for animals despite the costs of inactivity and vulnerability?

rows.t: Why are there critical periods for language learning?
rows.st: Why do children acquire languages with ease while adults struggle, and what closes that window in the brain?
Do humans produce and respond to pheromones that change behaviour or physiology, and if so which molecules are they?
Which genetic and environmental factors cause schizophrenia, and how do they produce its symptoms in the brain?
Which genes and environmental factors cause autism, and is there a biomarker that allows early diagnosis?

rows.t: To what extent can we stave off Alzheimer's?
rows.st: Can the onset of Alzheimer's disease be delayed by five to ten years with hormones, antioxidants, lifestyle or other treatments?

rows.t: What is the biological basis of addiction?
rows.st: How do drugs reshape the brain's reward circuitry, and how do personality and genes make some people far more vulnerable to addiction?

rows.t: Is morality hardwired into the brain?
rows.st: Are moral judgements produced by dedicated brain circuits that evolved for the purpose, and can imaging identify them?

rows.t: What are the limits of learning by machines?
rows.st: Is there a ceiling to what machines can learn from data, and can they reach the abstract reasoning humans show?

rows.t: How much of personality is genetic?
rows.st: What share of variation in human personality traits comes from genes, and how do genes and environment interact to shape them?

rows.t: What is the biological root of sexual orientation?
rows.st: Which prenatal hormonal, genetic and developmental factors shape sexual orientation in humans, and how much does each contribute?

rows.t: Will there ever be a tree of life that systematists can agree on?
rows.st: Can molecular and morphological data be reconciled into a single phylogenetic tree of all life that systematists accept?

rows.t: How many species are there on Earth?
rows.st: How many species of organisms live on Earth today, given that only about two million have been described?
Is there one definition of a species that works across sexual and asexual organisms, hybrids and lineages that exchange genes?

rows.t: Why does lateral transfer occur in so many species and how?
rows.st: Why is horizontal gene transfer so common among microbes, how does it happen and what does it do to fitness?

rows.t: Who was LUCA, the last universal common ancestor?
rows.st: What kind of organism was the last universal common ancestor of all life, when did it live and what genes did it carry?
How did flowering plants arise and diversify so fast, the question Darwin called an abominable mystery?

rows.t: How do plants make cell walls?
rows.st: How do plants synthesise and assemble cellulose, pectin and lignin into walls, and can that knowledge turn biomass into fuel?
Which genetic and hormonal controls let a redwood grow 100 metres while an arctic willow stays at ten centimetres?

rows.t: Why aren't all plants immune to all diseases?
rows.st: Why do plants, which have both general and specific immune responses, still fall to particular pathogens?

rows.t: What is the basis of variation in stress tolerance in plants?
rows.st: Which genes let some plants tolerate drought, cold and salt, and can those traits be bred into crops?
What triggered each of the five great mass extinctions, beyond the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs?
Can enough endangered species be saved at acceptable cost through politically feasible conservation to stop the current extinction wave?

rows.t: Why were some dinosaurs so large?
rows.st: How did sauropod dinosaurs grow to 100 tonnes and more within a few decades, and why were they so much larger than any land mammal?

rows.t: How will ecosystems respond to global warming?
rows.st: How will species ranges, food webs and ecosystem services shift as regional climates warm, and can the changes be predicted?

rows.t: How many kinds of humans coexisted in the recent past?
rows.st: How many human species lived during the past 100,000 years, and how did they interact with one another and with modern humans?

rows.t: What gave rise to modern human behavior?
rows.st: Did abstract thought, language and art emerge gradually in Homo sapiens or in a sudden cultural change, and what caused it?

rows.t: What are the roots of human culture?
rows.st: What lets humans accumulate culture by building on earlier discoveries in a way no other animal does?

rows.t: What are the evolutionary roots of language and music?
rows.st: How and why did language and music evolve in humans, and what neural changes made them possible?

rows.t: What are human races, and how did they develop?
rows.st: How does human genetic variation map onto geographic ancestry, and how did that structure arise from migration and selection?

rows.t: Why do some countries grow and others stagnate?
rows.st: What explains the large and persistent differences in economic growth and living standards between countries?

rows.t: What impact do large government deficits have on interest rates and growth?
rows.st: How do sustained large government deficits affect a country's interest rates and its long-run rate of economic growth?

rows.t: Are political and economic freedom closely tied?
rows.st: Does economic liberalisation lead to political freedom, or can authoritarian states sustain market economies indefinitely?

rows.t: Why has poverty increased and life expectancy declined in sub-Saharan Africa?
rows.st: Why did poverty rise and life expectancy fall in sub-Saharan Africa through the 1990s, and what interventions reverse the trend?

rows.t: What makes prime numbers so special?
rows.st: Why do the prime numbers, the building blocks of the integers, show the distribution and structure they do, and what governs their gaps?

rows.t: Will the periodic table ever be complete?
rows.st: Is there a last chemical element, and can elements beyond 118 be synthesised and shown to behave as the periodic table predicts?

rows.t: Are there more color pigments to discover?
rows.st: Can new stable inorganic pigments be found, as the blue YInMn pigment was in 2009, to fill colour gaps left by toxic or fading pigments?

rows.t: How can we measure interface phenomena on the microscopic level?
rows.st: Can chemical processes at solid-liquid and solid-gas interfaces be measured at atomic resolution under operating conditions?

rows.t: What is the future for energy storage?
rows.st: Which battery chemistries and storage technologies can store energy at the density, cost and lifetime a renewable grid and electric transport need?
Why does biology use only one handedness of amino acids and sugars, and could life work with the mirror set or a mixture?

rows.t: How can we better manage the world's plastic waste?
rows.st: Can plastics be made recyclable or degradable at scale so that waste stops accumulating in soil and oceans?

rows.t: Will AI redefine the future of chemistry?
rows.st: Can machine learning plan syntheses, predict reactivity and discover molecules and materials faster than human chemists?

rows.t: How can matter be programmed into living materials?
rows.st: Can engineered cells and synthetic components be combined into materials that grow, sense and repair themselves like living tissue?

rows.t: What drives reproduction in living systems?
rows.st: What is the physical and chemical principle that makes self-reproduction possible in living systems, from cells to organisms?

rows.t: Can we predict the next pandemic?
rows.st: Can surveillance and modelling identify which pathogen will cause the next pandemic early enough to prevent it?

rows.t: Will we ever find a cure for the common cold?
rows.st: Can a treatment or vaccine protect against the hundreds of rhinoviruses and other viruses that cause the common cold?

rows.t: Can we design and manufacture medicines customized for individual people?
rows.st: Can medicines be designed and made for one patient's genome and disease at a cost and speed that health systems can afford?

rows.t: Can a human tissue or organ be fully regenerated?
rows.st: Can a complete human organ such as a heart, kidney or limb be regrown in the body or built from a patient's own cells?

rows.t: How is immune homeostasis maintained and regulated?
rows.st: How does the immune system hold its balance between attacking pathogens and tolerating self and harmless antigens?

rows.t: Is there a scientific basis to the Meridian System in traditional Chinese medicine?
rows.st: Do the meridians of traditional Chinese medicine correspond to any measurable anatomical or physiological structure?

rows.t: How will the next generation of vaccines be made?
rows.st: Which platforms will produce the next vaccines, and can they be designed and manufactured within months of a new pathogen appearing?

rows.t: What is the etiology of autism?
rows.st: What combination of genetic variants and environmental exposures causes autism spectrum disorder, and through which neural changes?

rows.t: Can we ever overcome antibiotic resistance?
rows.st: Can new antibiotics, alternative therapies and stewardship together outpace the evolution of resistance in bacterial pathogens for good?

rows.t: What role does our microbiome play in health and disease?
rows.st: Which effects of the human microbiome on health and disease are causal, and can changing the microbiome treat disease?

rows.t: Can xenotransplantation solve the shortage of donor organs?
rows.st: Can genetically modified pig organs be transplanted into humans and function for years without rejection or infection?

rows.t: What could help conservation of the oceans?
rows.st: Which policies and technologies can end overfishing, acidification, warming and pollution of the oceans before ecosystems collapse?

rows.t: Can we stop ourselves from aging?
rows.st: Can the biological processes of aging be slowed or halted in humans, as they have been in laboratory animals?

rows.t: Why can only some cells become other cells?
rows.st: Why do stem cells keep the ability to change fate while most differentiated cells lose it, and what locks a cell's identity?

rows.t: Why are some genomes so big and others so small?
rows.st: What explains the thousandfold variation in genome size among organisms of comparable complexity, and is the extra DNA functional?

rows.t: Will it be possible to cure all cancers?
rows.st: Can every cancer be cured or controlled, given the diversity of tumours and their capacity to evolve resistance?

rows.t: What genes make us uniquely human?
rows.st: Which genes and regulatory changes distinguish humans from other primates and explain human-specific traits such as language and large brains?

rows.t: How do migratory animals know where they're going?
rows.st: Which senses and brain mechanisms guide migrating animals over thousands of kilometres to a precise destination?

rows.t: Why did dinosaurs grow to be so big?
rows.st: What physiology and ecology allowed sauropod dinosaurs to reach sizes far beyond any land animal before or since?

rows.t: How many species are there on Earth, 2021 list
rows.st: What is the total number of species alive on Earth, and how can it be estimated when most remain undescribed?
How do complex organs such as eyes and placentas arise by natural selection, and which puzzles in evolutionary theory remain?

rows.t: Why do humans get so attached to dogs and cats?
rows.st: What biological and psychological mechanisms create the strong bond between humans and their companion animals?
Can an extinct species be brought back by cloning, genome editing or back-breeding, and would the result count as the original species?
Which brain systems generate emotions, and are emotions discrete categories or constructed from more basic affective dimensions?

rows.t: Will the world's population keep growing indefinitely?
rows.st: When and at what level will the human population peak, and what drives the fertility decline that would end its growth?
What signals end growth at the right adult size, closing the growth plates and halting cell proliferation?
Can a torpor or hibernation state be induced safely in humans for medicine or long spaceflight?

rows.t: Will humans look physically different in the future?
rows.st: Will natural selection, culture and technology change human bodies measurably over coming millennia, and in what direction?

rows.t: Why were there species explosions and mass extinctions?
rows.st: What drives the bursts of diversification and the mass extinctions seen in the fossil record?

rows.t: How might genome editing be used to cure disease?
rows.st: Can CRISPR and related tools correct disease-causing mutations safely in patients, and for which diseases?

rows.t: Can a cell be artificially synthesized?
rows.st: Can a living cell be built from nonliving chemical components rather than copied from an existing cell?

rows.t: How are biomolecules organized in cells to function in order?
rows.st: How do cells arrange thousands of molecules in space and time so that reactions happen in the right place and order?

rows.t: How many dimensions are there in space?
rows.st: Does space have more than three dimensions, as string theory proposes, and could extra dimensions be detected?

rows.t: What is the shape of the universe?
rows.st: Is the universe spatially flat, open or closed, and is it finite or infinite in extent?

rows.t: Where did the Big Bang start?
rows.st: Did the big bang have a location or an initial state, and what, if anything, preceded the hot dense beginning of the universe?

rows.t: Is it possible to live permanently on another planet?
rows.st: Can humans build a self-sustaining permanent settlement on Mars or another body in the solar system?
How do black holes form and grow, including the supermassive ones found early in cosmic history, and what is inside them?

rows.t: What is the universe made of, 2021 list
rows.st: What are dark matter and dark energy, and what is the full inventory of matter and energy in the universe?

rows.t: Why don't the orbits of planets decay and cause collisions?
rows.st: Is the solar system stable over billions of years, or can planetary orbits become chaotic enough for collisions?

rows.t: When will the universe die? Will it continue to expand?
rows.st: Will the expansion of the universe continue forever, and what final state does it approach?

rows.t: What is the origin of cosmic rays?
rows.st: Which sources accelerate cosmic rays across their energy range, from galactic supernova remnants to the highest energies?

rows.t: Are we alone in the universe, 2021 list
rows.st: Does life exist beyond Earth, and can it be detected through biosignatures on exoplanets or signals from technological civilisations?

rows.t: What is the origin of mass?
rows.st: What gives elementary particles their masses, and why do the masses take the values they do?

rows.t: Is our Milky Way Galaxy special?
rows.st: Is the Milky Way typical among galaxies of its kind, or unusual in its history, satellites or disk structure?

rows.t: What is the smallest scale of space-time?
rows.st: Is spacetime continuous down to arbitrarily small scales, or does it become discrete or foamlike near the Planck length?

rows.t: Is Einstein's general theory of relativity correct?
rows.st: Does general relativity hold in strong fields and at cosmological scales, or does it break down where dark energy or quantum effects appear?

rows.t: Is water necessary for all life in the universe, or just on Earth?
rows.st: Could life use a solvent other than water, or is water a requirement for life anywhere?
How do neutron stars acquire the fast rotation and strong magnetic fields that make them pulsars, and how do they emit?

rows.t: What is preventing humans from carrying out deep-space exploration?
rows.st: Which technical, biological and economic barriers stop humans travelling beyond the Moon, and how can they be overcome?

rows.t: What is the volume, composition, and significance of the deep biosphere?
rows.st: How much life lives deep in Earth's crust and sediments, what organisms make it up and how does it affect the planet?

rows.t: Will humans one day have to leave the planet?
rows.st: Will changes to Earth or the Sun force humans to leave the planet, and could they survive elsewhere?

rows.t: Is it possible to understand the structure of compact stars and matter?
rows.st: What is the equation of state of matter inside neutron stars, and do quark or other exotic phases appear at their cores?

rows.t: What is the origin of high-energy cosmic neutrinos?
rows.st: Which astrophysical sources produce the high-energy neutrinos detected by IceCube, and how do they accelerate the parent particles?
What is gravity at the quantum level, and how does the curvature of spacetime emerge from a deeper theory?

rows.t: Where do the heavy elements in the universe come from?
rows.st: Which astrophysical events make the elements heavier than iron, and in what proportions do neutron star mergers and supernovae contribute?
Is the diffraction limit a hard bound on optical resolution, or can imaging and lithography go below it in general?

rows.t: What is the microscopic mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity?
rows.st: What microscopic interaction produces superconductivity above 30 kelvin in cuprate, iron-based and nickelate materials, and can it be designed?

rows.t: What are the limits of heat transfer in matter?
rows.st: Are there fundamental upper and lower bounds on thermal conductivity in solids, and what sets them?

rows.t: What are the fundamental principles of collective motion?
rows.st: Is there a general theory for the collective motion of flocks, swarms and active matter made of self-propelled units?

rows.t: Will we ever travel at the speed of light?
rows.st: Can massive objects approach light speed or bypass the limit through spacetime geometry, or is interstellar travel bound to slow speeds?

rows.t: What is quantum uncertainty and why is it important?
rows.st: What does the uncertainty principle say about reality rather than about measurement, and what deeper structure does it reflect?

rows.t: What are the smallest building blocks of matter?
rows.st: Are quarks, leptons and bosons fundamental, or are they made of smaller constituents or strings?

rows.t: Why does time seem to flow in only one direction?
rows.st: Why does time have an arrow when the fundamental laws are nearly symmetric under time reversal?

rows.t: Are there any particles that behave oppositely to photons?
rows.st: Is there a particle whose properties mirror those of the photon, such as a magnetic monopole or a dark photon?

rows.t: What is the maximum speed to which we can accelerate a particle?
rows.st: Is there a practical or fundamental ceiling to the energy particle accelerators can reach, on Earth or in cosmic sources?

rows.t: Will Bose-Einstein condensates see wide use in the future?
rows.st: Can Bose-Einstein condensates move from laboratories into sensors, clocks and quantum devices in wide use?

rows.t: Can we accurately simulate the macro- and microworld?
rows.st: Can quantum and classical simulation reproduce matter from electrons to materials accurately enough to replace experiment?

rows.t: Can humans make intense lasers with incoherence comparable to sunlight?
rows.st: Can a laser be built that is both intense and as incoherent as sunlight, for applications that need both?

rows.t: Is quantum many-body entanglement more fundamental than quantum fields?
rows.st: Does spacetime and field structure emerge from patterns of quantum entanglement, or are fields the more fundamental description?

rows.t: Can we make a real, human-size invisibility cloak?
rows.st: Can metamaterials or other methods hide a human-sized object across visible wavelengths and viewing angles?

rows.t: Will there ever be a theory of everything?
rows.st: Can all forces and particles be described by one theory, and would it be testable?
What is the dark matter that outweighs ordinary matter five to one, and can it be detected directly?

rows.t: What is the optimum hardware for quantum computers?
rows.st: Which physical platform, superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, neutral atom or topological, can scale to fault-tolerant quantum computing?

rows.t: What is the ultimate statistical invariance of turbulence?
rows.st: Which statistical properties of turbulent flow are universal across scales and systems, and can they be derived from the Navier-Stokes equations?

rows.t: How can we develop manufacturing systems on Mars?
rows.st: Can materials and parts be manufactured on Mars from local resources to support human presence there?

rows.t: How can we break the current limit on energy-conversion efficiencies?
rows.st: Can energy converters such as solar cells, engines and fuel cells be pushed past their present efficiency ceilings?

rows.t: Is a future of only self-driving cars realistic?
rows.st: Can autonomous vehicles reach safety and generality to replace human drivers entirely on public roads?

rows.t: Is there an upper limit to computer processing speed?
rows.st: Do physics and architecture set a hard ceiling on how fast a computer can process information?

rows.t: Can DNA act as an information storage medium?
rows.st: Can DNA store digital data at scale with the density, durability and cost needed for archival storage?
Can artificial intelligence diagnose and manage patients as well as physicians across the breadth of medicine?

rows.t: Can topological quantum computing be realized?
rows.st: Can non-abelian anyons be created and braided in a solid-state device to make fault-tolerant topological qubits?
Which brain structures and processes generate conscious experience, and how could their role be established?

rows.t: What are the coding principles embedded in neuronal spike trains?
rows.st: How do sequences of neuronal spikes encode information, by rate, timing, synchrony or population patterns?

rows.t: Can human memory be stored, manipulated, and transplanted digitally?
rows.st: Can the content of a human memory be read out, edited or transferred to a machine or another brain?
