What does sleep do for the brain and body that cannot be done while awake, making it a necessity across animals?

rows.t: What is addiction and how does it work?
rows.st: What changes in brain circuits turn drug use into compulsion, and why does it happen to some people and not others?

rows.t: Why do we fall in love?
rows.st: Which neural and hormonal processes produce romantic love, and what evolutionary function does it serve?
Can Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and other neurodegenerative diseases be stopped or reversed in patients rather than slowed by a fraction?
What genetic and developmental causes make about 90 percent of humans right-handed, a bias no other species shares so strongly?

rows.t: Is it possible to predict the future?
rows.st: Can advanced machines predict social and natural events far ahead, as orbital mechanics predicts the motion of stars and satellites?

rows.t: How did speech evolve and what parts of the brain control it?
rows.st: When and how did speech evolve in the human lineage, and which brain regions control its production and comprehension?
What cognitive abilities do other animals have, and how can intelligence be compared across species with different bodies and senses?

rows.t: Can we better diagnose and treat complex mental disorders?
rows.st: Can biomarkers and mechanism-based treatments replace symptom checklists for disorders such as depression and schizophrenia?

rows.t: Can we stop global climate change?
rows.st: Can emissions be cut fast enough to hold warming below the Paris Agreement limits, and which policies and technologies achieve it?

rows.t: Where do we put all the excess carbon dioxide?
rows.st: Can captured carbon dioxide be stored or used at the gigatonne scale needed, and where can it go safely?

rows.t: What creates the Earth's magnetic field?
rows.st: How does the geodynamo in Earth's liquid outer core generate the magnetic field, and why do the poles wander and reverse?

rows.t: Will we be able to predict catastrophic weather events more accurately?
rows.st: Can tsunamis, hurricanes and earthquakes be forecast with the lead time and accuracy needed to save lives?

rows.t: What happens if all the ice on the planet melts?
rows.st: How much would sea level rise and how would climate change if all land ice melted, and on what timescale could that occur?

rows.t: Can we create an environmentally friendly replacement for plastics?
rows.st: Can a material match the cost and performance of commodity plastics while degrading harmlessly or recycling fully?

rows.t: Can we achieve a situation where every material can be recycled and reused?
rows.st: Can a circular economy be built in which every material is recovered and reused rather than discarded?

rows.t: Will we soon see the end of monocultures like wheat, maize, rice, and soy?
rows.st: Can agriculture move away from a few monoculture crops without losing yield, and will it?

rows.t: Could we live in a fossil-fuel-free world?
rows.st: Can the world's energy, transport and industry run entirely without fossil fuels, and by when?

rows.t: What is the future of hydrogen energy?
rows.st: Can hydrogen be produced, stored and used cleanly at a cost that makes it a major energy carrier?

rows.t: Will cold fusion ever be possible?
rows.st: Can nuclear fusion occur at room temperature in condensed matter, as claimed in 1989 and never reproduced?

rows.t: Will injectable, disease-fighting nanobots ever be a reality?
rows.st: Can nanoscale machines be injected into the body to find and treat disease at the cellular level?

rows.t: Is there a limit to human intelligence?
rows.st: Do biology and physics set a ceiling on human intelligence, and could it be raised by evolution or technology?

rows.t: Will it be possible to create sentient robots?
rows.st: Can a machine be built that has subjective experience, and how would anyone establish that it does?
Will artificial intelligence surpass humans at most economically valuable work, and what follows for human roles?

rows.t: Could we integrate with computers to form a human-machine hybrid species?
rows.st: Can brain-computer interfaces merge human cognition with machines far enough to create a hybrid form of intelligence?
How does collective intelligence arise from interacting individuals in insect swarms, markets and human groups, and what are its limits?

rows.t: Can robots or AIs have human creativity?
rows.st: Can artificial systems be creative in the way humans are, producing novel and valuable ideas rather than recombinations?

rows.t: Can quantum artificial intelligence imitate the human brain?
rows.st: Could quantum computers run learning algorithms that reproduce the capabilities of the human brain better than classical machines?
Can a privately financed team build and fly a reusable spacecraft carrying three people to 100 kilometres altitude twice within two weeks?
Can a small team build a rocket vehicle that takes off vertically, hovers, translates and lands precisely in a simulated lunar descent profile?
Can 100 whole human genomes be sequenced within 30 days at an audited cost of 1,000 dollars each with one error per million bases and 98 percent completeness?
Can a production-capable car achieve 100 miles per gallon equivalent with under 200 grams per mile of well-to-wheel carbon dioxide emissions?
Can a privately funded team land a rover on the Moon, travel 500 metres and transmit high-definition video back to Earth?
Can a device skim crude oil from seawater at 2,500 gallons per minute with 70 percent efficiency, far faster than existing cleanup technology?
Can a consumer device weighing under five pounds diagnose 13 medical conditions and capture five vital signs as well as a panel of physicians?
Can new sensors and sensing systems let people monitor their health and gather medical data outside the clinic?
Can affordable, accurate and stable pH sensors be built to measure ocean acidification in the field over long deployments?
Can open-source tablet software teach children in developing countries to read, write and do arithmetic on their own within 15 months?
Can autonomous systems map at least 250 square kilometres of seafloor at 4,000 metres depth at five metre resolution within 24 hours?
Can a mobile application raise the reading proficiency of low-literate adults measurably within 12 months of use?
Can carbon dioxide from a working coal or gas power plant flue be converted into products with the highest net value at scale?

rows.t: Anu and Naveen Jain Women's Safety XPRIZE
rows.st: Can a wearable device trigger an emergency alert autonomously and inconspicuously and transmit information to community responders within 90 seconds?
Can teams demonstrate artificial intelligence applications that address grand challenges for humanity, judged by their impact?
Can a robotic avatar let an operator see, hear, move and manipulate objects at a remote site in real time as if present there?
Can COVID-19 tests be made faster, cheaper and easier to use at scale within six months of the pandemic's start?
Can AI systems predict COVID-19 infection rates by region and prescribe intervention plans that balance cases against economic cost?
Can plant or cell-based alternatives match chicken breast or fish fillet in taste, texture, nutrition and cost?
Can a team demonstrate removal of at least 1,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year from air or oceans with a credible path to gigatonne scale?
Can an affordable, accurate and fast point-of-care test tell bacterial from other infections and guide antibiotic choice anywhere in the world?

rows.t: Dietary cause of scurvy and rickets
rows.st: Which missing food factors cause scurvy and rickets, diseases that John Snow attributed in 1857 to bread adulteration, and can feeding experiments isolate the substance that prevents them?
What causes rickets in children, which John Snow blamed in 1857 on alum added to bread, and does a dietary factor or sunlight explain the disease?
Can a solid-state device made of a semiconductor amplify electrical signals, as Lilienfeld's field-effect concept of 1925 proposed, and what materials and surface treatments make it work?
Can a steam engine drive a full-size vehicle on rails, as William Reynolds proposed around 1787, and can a high-pressure engine be light enough to avoid breaking the track?
Can a rocket burn liquid fuel and oxidiser fed from tanks, as Oberth's 1923 book suggested, and can a working vehicle be built to fly under its own power?
When a cell divides, does each strand of the DNA double helix serve as a template for a new partner strand, as the 1953 structure suggested, or is replication conservative or dispersive?

rows.t: First codon of the genetic code
rows.st: Which nucleotide triplet codes for which amino acid, the question Gamow and the RNA Tie Club took up in 1954, and what first codon can be read with a synthetic RNA?

rows.t: Mapping of codons to amino acids
rows.st: How are all sixty-four nucleotide triplets assigned to the twenty amino acids and stop signals, a coding problem the RNA Tie Club posed in 1954 and experiments could now solve?
Can an RNA molecule catalyse its own copying without any protein, as the RNA world proposal of 1962 requires, and what chemical conditions would let a self-replicating RNA arise?
Do microscopic living organisms exist that are invisible to the eye and cause infectious disease, as Kircher argued in 1658, and can a microscope show them directly?
Can the nucleus of an adult mammalian cell direct the development of a whole new animal, as Gurdon's 1958 frog cloning suggested for amphibians, and how would it be done in sheep?

rows.t: Gene therapy in a human patient
rows.st: Can a functional gene supplied from outside replace a defective one in a patient, as Rogers proposed in 1970, and can it be delivered safely to human cells?
Can immunisation protect people against tuberculosis, as Robert Koch proposed in 1890, and which weakened strain of the bacterium would be safe enough to use as a vaccine?
Are anthrax and similar diseases caused by living microbes carried between hosts, as Fracastoro proposed in 1546, and can a specific bacterium be tied to a specific disease?
How does the body come to make antibodies that fit a particular foreign substance, a question Ehrlich's side-chain theory of 1900 raised, and does the antigen select a pre-existing cell?

rows.t: Number of molecules in a mole
rows.st: How many molecules does a given volume of gas hold, if equal volumes contain equal numbers as Avogadro proposed in 1811, and can that number be measured?

rows.t: Uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus
rows.st: What neutral component of the nucleus, suggested by Rutherford in 1920, accounts for atomic masses exceeding the proton count, and can its penetrating radiation be identified?
Do positively charged carbon intermediates exist in organic reactions, as Stieglitz proposed in 1899, and can a medium be found in which one lives long enough to be observed directly?
Can sixty carbon atoms form a stable closed cage shaped like a soccer ball, as Osawa predicted in 1970, and what third form of carbon beyond graphite and diamond results?
Does an undiscovered element sit below boron in the periodic table with an atomic mass near 44, as Mendeleev predicted for eka-boron in 1871, and can spectroscopy find it?
Does a seventh noble gas with atomic number 118 exist, as Bohr's 1922 electron-shell scheme implies, and can heavy-ion collisions produce a few atoms of it?
Can the metal hidden in alum and clay be isolated from its compounds, as Davy attempted around 1808, and by what chemical or electrical route?
Can iron alloyed with chromium resist corrosion well enough for cutlery and tools, as Berthier noted in 1821, and what composition gives a practical rust-proof steel?
Can a lightweight polymer fibre be made strong and stiff enough to reinforce tyres, the goal of Kwolek's group at DuPont from 1964, and how can it be spun?

rows.t: Collapse of a massive star into a black hole
rows.st: Can a sufficiently massive star become so dense that light cannot escape, as Laplace suggested in 1796, and what does general relativity say about the collapse of a star above the neutron-star limit?

rows.t: Upper mass limit of neutron stars
rows.st: Is there a maximum mass above which a neutron star cannot support itself against gravity, a question that arose once Baade and Zwicky proposed such stars in 1933?
What source produces the rapid, extremely regular radio pulses found in 1967, and can a rotating magnetised neutron star, as Pacini suggested that year, explain them?
Why do stars in spiral galaxies orbit faster than the visible mass allows, an anomaly Oort first reported in 1932 for the Milky Way, and does it hold at large distances?
Is the relic radiation of the hot early universe, predicted in 1948 by Alpher and Herman, a perfect black body, and can a spectrometer above the atmosphere show it?
Do giant planets orbit Sun-like stars much closer than Mercury orbits the Sun, as Struve argued in 1952 was possible, and could periodic Doppler shifts of the star reveal one?
What is the mass of the Earth, a question the 1774 Schiehallion experiment began to answer by measuring plumb-line deflection, and can a laboratory torsion balance measure it more precisely?
Does Saturn's moon Titan hold an atmosphere, as limb darkening seen by Comas i Sola in 1903 suggested, and can a spectrum of the moon confirm which gas it contains?
Does a belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune, as Fernandez proposed in 1980, supply the short-period comets, and do orbital simulations of such a belt reproduce the observed comet orbits?
Does Uranus have a ring system, as William Herschel suspected in 1789, and can a stellar occultation reveal narrow rings too faint to see directly?
Does the magnetic field of the Earth trap energetic charged particles in belts around the planet, a possibility explored since 1895, and can a satellite detector find them?
Does the rotation of the Andromeda galaxy follow the visible mass, or does it imply extra unseen matter, as Babcock's 1939 rotation measurements suggested for its outer regions?
Can a set of weak learners, each only slightly better than random guessing, be combined into one strong learner, the question Kearns and Valiant posed in 1988, and by what algorithm?
Can undirected connectivity be decided in logarithmic memory, when Savitch's theorem of 1970 gave only log-squared space, and does randomness or a deterministic construction close the gap?
Can data be encrypted so that arbitrary computations run on the ciphertext, a problem first posed in 1978, and can a scheme be made fast enough to use in practice?

rows.t: Double-spend-free digital cash without a trusted party
rows.st: Can digital cash that cannot be spent twice work without a trusted bank, as the b-money and bit gold proposals of 1998 sought, and what agreement mechanism prevents double spending?
Can a practical public-key encryption scheme be built from a one-way trapdoor function, the concept Diffie and Hellman published in 1976 without giving an implementation?

rows.t: Practical codes near the Shannon limit
rows.st: Is there a practical error-correcting code that operates within a fraction of a decibel of the channel capacity Shannon stated in 1948, with decoding that runs in reasonable time?
Can an explicit code with efficient encoding and decoding provably achieve the channel capacity that Shannon stated in 1948, without a random construction or an exhaustive search?

rows.t: Machine victory over the world chess champion
rows.st: Can a computer program defeat the human world chess champion, an outcome a Carnegie Mellon team predicted in 1957 would come within ten years, and what search power is needed?
Can a neural network more than a thousand layers deep be trained despite the vanishing gradients Hochreiter identified in 1991 and the degradation of accuracy as layers are added?
Can a learning system reach grandmaster level at the real-time strategy game StarCraft II, which commentators in 2015 expected to follow in five to ten years from DeepMind's research?
Is there a general procedure that decides whether a given program or tag system halts, a candidate for unsolvability that Post examined in 1920, and can it be proved impossible?
Can a quantum computer perform a calculation that no classical computer can finish in feasible time, a goal that follows from the 1980 and 1981 proposals of Manin and Feynman?

rows.t: Recording electrical activity from the human brain
rows.st: Can the electrical activity of the living human brain be recorded through the intact scalp, as Caton recorded it from exposed animal brains in 1875, and what rhythms does it show?
Which gene on which chromosome causes Huntington's disease, a hunt for which the Hereditary Disease Foundation was founded in 1968, and can linkage analysis locate it?
Can mental ability be measured with a standardised test, as Galton tried in his testing centre from 1882, and can such a test predict which children need special schooling?
Does the adult brain reorganise itself with experience, as William James suggested in 1890, and what rule for strengthening connections between neurons could produce such change?
Is the nervous system made of separate nerve cells, in line with Schwann's 1839 cell theory, or is it a continuous network, and can staining show the boundaries between cells?
Is the hydrogen nucleus a building block of every nucleus, as Prout's hypothesis of 1815 held for atomic weights, and can a particle identified in nuclear reactions be shown to be that unit?
Does a negatively charged counterpart of the proton exist, as Dirac suggested in his 1933 Nobel lecture, and can an accelerator produce enough energy to create and detect it?
Is there a second kind of neutrino, distinct from the one in beta decay, as the two-meson theory of Sakata and Inoue in 1942 implied, and can an experiment tell them apart?
Does a baryon made of three strange quarks exist with the mass that Okubo and Gell-Mann predicted in 1961 from the eightfold way, and what decay products would show it?
Does a sixth quark flavour called top exist, as Kobayashi and Maskawa's three-generation scheme of 1973 requires to explain CP violation, and how heavy must it be to have escaped detection?
Do isotopes of one element differ in nuclear composition, as Soddy suggested in 1913 from decay chains, and what makes up the extra mass in the heavier isotope?

rows.t: Light from fast particles in liquids
rows.st: Do charged particles moving faster than light in a medium emit a cone of light, as Heaviside argued in 1888, and can the faint blue glow in liquids be shown to have this origin?
Are the 2S and 2P levels of hydrogen exactly equal, as the Dirac equation says, or is there a small splitting like the one Pasternack proposed in 1938 that microwaves could measure?
Can an electron and a positron form a short-lived bound atom, as Mohorovicic predicted in 1934, and can it be made and observed in the laboratory?
Can stimulated emission, which Einstein proposed in 1917, be used to amplify microwaves coherently, and what arrangement of molecules would sustain the process?

rows.t: Bose-Einstein condensate in a dilute gas
rows.st: Can a dilute gas of bosonic atoms cooled close to absolute zero collapse into one quantum state, as Einstein predicted in 1924 from Bose's statistics, and how can it be reached?
Does light travel at a finite speed, a question Galileo tried to test in 1638 with lanterns on distant hills, and can astronomical timing measure that speed?
Why is the daytime sky blue, a question Leonardo da Vinci answered around 1506 by conjecturing that small particles scatter sunlight, and what quantitative law governs the scattering?
Does light exert a measurable pressure on a surface, as Maxwell's electromagnetic theory of 1862 implies, and can an experiment detect a force that small?
Why does the orbit of Mercury precess 43 arcseconds per century faster than Newtonian gravity predicts, an excess Le Verrier flagged in 1859, and what theory accounts for it?
What physical property of the electron explains the two-valuedness Pauli identified in 1924 in the spectra of atoms, and does it correspond to an actual rotation of the electron?

rows.t: Why is the equity risk premium so high?
rows.st: Why have stocks earned a premium of five to eight percent a year over government bonds, a gap that standard economic models cannot explain?

rows.t: Why do national savings and investment rates correlate?
rows.st: Why are domestic saving and domestic investment so strongly correlated across countries when capital can move freely to the best return worldwide?

rows.t: Why does capital not flow from rich to poor countries?
rows.st: Why does capital not flow from developed to developing countries, although poor countries have less capital per worker and so should offer higher returns?

rows.t: Why does the high-interest currency appreciate?
rows.st: Why does a currency with a higher interest rate tend to appreciate, when uncovered interest parity predicts it should depreciate by the rate difference?

rows.t: Why is consumption uncorrelated with the real exchange rate?
rows.st: Why is the correlation between relative consumption and the real exchange rate near zero or negative, when full international risk sharing predicts a positive one?
Why do corporations pay dividends and why do investors pay attention to them, when dividends are taxed more heavily than capital gains?

rows.t: Why is the credit rating market so concentrated?
rows.st: What explains the concentrated market structure of credit rating agencies, where a few firms rate most of the world's debt?

rows.t: What is the definition of disease?
rows.st: Is there a definition of disease that fits both the physiological process behind it and the patient's suffering and loss of quality of life?

rows.t: How can evidence-based medicine guide care of an individual?
rows.st: How can results from trials on large samples of patients be applied to the care of one individual patient in evidence-based medicine?

rows.t: What causes idiopathic diseases such as aggressive periodontitis?
rows.st: What causes diseases of unknown origin, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or aggressive periodontitis, and can treatment be found before the cause is?

rows.t: How do paracetamol, lithium and antidepressants work?
rows.st: By what mechanism do paracetamol, antidepressants and lithium relieve symptoms, even though their effects on certain biological processes are known?

rows.t: Where is the next proton magic number beyond lead?
rows.st: Which proton number gives the next closed nuclear shell for superheavy elements, given that estimates range from 114 to 126 and agreement is lacking?

rows.t: How does nitrogenase catalyse nitrogen reduction?
rows.st: By what step-by-step mechanism does the nitrogenase enzyme reduce atmospheric nitrogen to ammonia at its iron-molybdenum cofactor?

rows.t: How does the manganese cluster oxidise water in photosystem II?
rows.st: Where and by what mechanism does the four-manganese, one-calcium cluster of photosystem II oxidise water, and can that mechanism be copied in artificial photosynthesis?

rows.t: What is the origin of the hydrophobic effect?
rows.st: What physical interactions make non-polar molecules cluster in water, and what is the origin of the hydrophobic effect that drives protein folding?

rows.t: What role does induced fit play in enzyme fidelity?
rows.st: How much does induced fit contribute to the accuracy of enzymes that copy or process substrates, and how can its role be defined and measured?

rows.t: What are the chemical properties of the transactinide elements?
rows.st: What are the chemical properties of the transactinide elements, which have been predicted by theory but not yet measured experimentally?

rows.t: How do charge-assisted hydrogen bonds relate to ionic and covalent bonds?
rows.st: How do unusually strong hydrogen bonds relate to conventional hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and covalent bonds, and where does one type of bonding end?

rows.t: Can metallic hydrogen be made and kept at lower pressure?
rows.st: Does a condensed metallic state of hydrogen exist at pressures far below those of the planetary interior, as some Rydberg matter claims say, and can it be reproduced?

rows.t: Do glassy ice phases connect to a second liquid water state?
rows.st: Is deep-glassy disordered ice a distinct amorphous phase, and does it point to two distinct liquid states of water at low temperature?

rows.t: Is there a true phase transition underlying the glass transition?
rows.st: Does a second-order phase transition lie behind the glass transition in the limit of infinitely long relaxation times, or is the transition purely kinetic?
Is there an online algorithm for the k-server problem in any metric space with competitive ratio exactly k, as the k-server conjecture states?

rows.t: Is matrix mortality decidable for two by two matrices?
rows.st: Is it decidable whether a finite set of two by two integer matrices has a product equal to the zero matrix, given that the problem is undecidable from three by three upward?

rows.t: Can a planted clique be found in polynomial time?
rows.st: Can a clique hidden in a random graph be found in polynomial time at intermediate clique sizes, or does the planted clique conjecture of hardness hold?

rows.t: Is every real-time computable irrational number transcendental?
rows.st: Can an irrational number whose digits a Turing machine writes in real time be algebraic, or must every such number be transcendental?

rows.t: Are all NP-complete languages polynomial-time isomorphic?
rows.st: Are all NP-complete languages related to one another by polynomial-time isomorphisms, as the Berman-Hartmanis conjecture says?

rows.t: How can machines acquire common sense reasoning?
rows.st: How can an AI system hold the broad everyday knowledge about objects and situations that people use, and reason with it as people do?

rows.t: How can humans supervise AI that outperforms them?
rows.st: How can people supervise an AI system that outperforms or misleads them in a domain, the scalable oversight problem of AI alignment?

rows.t: What is the computational complexity of the Shannon capacity of a graph?
rows.st: How hard is it to compute the Shannon capacity of a channel represented by a graph, which the Lovasz number bounds from above?

rows.t: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem?
rows.st: Is there a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem, whose solution would break many lattice-based cryptosystems?

rows.t: Are practical lattice cryptosystems as hard as worst-case lattice problems?
rows.st: Do the efficient lattice-based schemes, such as NTRU and LWE with practical parameters, have security reductions to worst-case lattice problems?

rows.t: What is the boundary problem of consciousness?
rows.st: What determines the boundary of a single conscious experience, and why does one unified field of experience stop where it does instead of merging with others?

rows.t: How does the brainstem modulate dream content?
rows.st: How does brainstem activation during sleep shape the content of dreams, and can the modulation described by the activation-synthesis hypothesis be measured quantitatively?

rows.t: How can non-physical qualia affect the brain?
rows.st: If subjective experiences are not physical, how could they have any effect on brain activity or behaviour, given that physical events seem to have complete physical causes?

rows.t: What is the neural source of the internal clock for time perception?
rows.st: What produces the pulses that the brain counts to estimate duration, and which brain structures or circuits implement the internal clock proposed by pacemaker-accumulator models?

rows.t: How does the adult brain perceive form from stationary viewing?
rows.st: How does the adult visual system recover the shape and form of an object from a stationary view, and which computations in visual cortex carry out this recognition?

rows.t: Why do some animals sleep with one brain hemisphere at a time?
rows.st: What is the function of unihemispheric slow-wave sleep in birds and aquatic mammals, and does the asymmetry seen in flying birds match that seen in resting ones?
By what mechanism does damage to the occipital or temporal lobes make a patient see two or more repeated images of a single object after fixation?

rows.t: What is the function of the cortisol awakening response?
rows.st: What is the biological function of the sharp rise in cortisol shortly after waking, and does it prepare the body for the stress of the coming day?

rows.t: Which metaphysical conclusion does the explanatory gap support?
rows.st: What does the difficulty of explaining how physical properties give rise to felt experience show about the nature of mind, and which metaphysical view should follow?

rows.t: What makes the human brain uniquely adapted to language?
rows.st: What feature of the human brain makes it uniquely suited to language, given that apes and monkeys have analogues of the same language regions?

rows.t: Which animals are capable of feeling pain?
rows.st: Which organisms are capable of experiencing pain, and what evidence from behaviour or neural structure could settle that question across the animal kingdom?

rows.t: What adaptive advantage does consciousness provide?
rows.st: What adaptive advantage could consciousness provide, if evolution cannot tell a conscious organism from a non-conscious one that performs the same function?

rows.t: Do animals dream under general anesthesia?
rows.st: Do animals dream while under general anesthesia, and can any measurable signal separate dreaming from unconsciousness in an anesthetized brain?
What causes the pain that most amputees feel in a limb that is gone, and does somatosensory cortex reorganisation or activation explain it?

rows.t: What causes phantom vibrations of a mobile phone?
rows.st: Why do people perceive their phone vibrating or ringing when it is not, and what cognitive or neural process produces the false sensation?
What causes posterior cortical atrophy, the visual variant of dementia, and what diagnostic criteria can the clinical community fully accept?

rows.t: Does recall create a new memory or retrieve a reconsolidated one?
rows.st: When an old situation is recalled, does the brain form a new memory or reconsolidate the original, and how could the two be told apart experimentally?

rows.t: What is the total capacity of long-term memory?
rows.st: How much information can long-term memory hold, and what measure of capacity applies to a biological memory system?

rows.t: What is the function of mirror neurons in macaques?
rows.st: What function do mirror neurons serve in macaques, which fire both when the animal acts and when it watches the same action?

rows.t: Do young children understand the syntactic rules of their language?
rows.st: At the stage of early two-word sentences, do children understand the underlying rules of their language, such as syntactic categories?

rows.t: Is there a consensus definition of autistic burnout?
rows.st: Can researchers agree on one definition and set of diagnostic features for autistic burnout, given the several competing characterisations proposed so far?

rows.t: Should large language models be viewed as models of the human mind?
rows.st: If and how should large language models be treated as models of the human brain or human mind, and what evidence would support such a claim?

rows.t: How can mental disorders be defined in a culturally neutral way?
rows.st: Can a definition of mental disorders be written that does not depend on the cultural norms of the Western authors of diagnostic manuals?

rows.t: Can mental disorders be classified by their cause?
rows.st: Can psychiatry group mental disorders by cause instead of by symptoms, as medicine does for paralysis or kidney failure, and would that improve treatment?

rows.t: Why is the diagnosis of major depression unreliable?
rows.st: Why do independent experts diagnose major depressive disorder inconsistently, with an agreement score near 0.28, and how can psychiatric diagnosis be made reliable?

rows.t: How do psychiatric medications help patients?
rows.st: Does a psychiatric drug correct a specific chemical imbalance, change the balance of brain activity, or only keep the patient manageable?
Do particles made of four quarks and one antiquark exist, as the quark model allowed from 1964, and can a collider experiment find them in baryon decays?

rows.t: What is the charge radius of the proton?
rows.st: Why did muonic hydrogen spectroscopy in 2010 give a proton charge radius about four percent smaller than electron scattering and hydrogen spectroscopy, and which value is right?

rows.t: Can a quantum system have a ground state in perpetual motion?
rows.st: Can a quantum system have a ground state in repeating motion, as Shapere and Wilczek proposed in 2012, given that only periodically driven discrete time crystals have been observed?
